All four suites pass: impl-1 35 tests, impl-2 28, impl-3 29, impl-4 27. I probed each one with throwaway tests and deleted them afterwards.

Shared flaws:
- After a failed submit with "Active" unchecked, the checkbox comes back checked. The prepareForValidation merge does not reach the flashed old input.
- Inactive products are still served at /products/{slug}.
- All four use the default Tailwind pagination view, which renders unstyled because there is no compiled CSS.

impl-3 ranks first:
- It is the only one with no N+1 on related products; it eager-loads category.
- Query-string input is validated, so array params never cause a 500.
- The model layer is the richest: scopes with tie-breakers, a formattedPrice accessor and an index.
- The shared form component is solid and there is a policy test.
- Its main flaw is UX: an invalid category or sort on the public GET redirects to the home page.

impl-4 ranks second. It is simple and clean, with a shared form component, a badge component and flash in the layout. It has three real bugs:
- Array query params cause a 500.
- An unknown sort drops ordering entirely.
- Related products cause an N+1.

impl-1 ranks third. It has the best query scopes and the best tests (datasets, assertInvalid). Its bugs:
- Slug auto-generation, which the spec did not ask for, returns a 500 when the name has no sluggable characters (e.g. "!!!").
- Related products cause an N+1.
- It has the same redirect-home behaviour on invalid filters as impl-3.
- Minor ceremony: #[UseFactory] plus a factory $model on top of HasFactory.

impl-2 ranks last:
- Array query params cause a 500.
- Related products cause an N+1.
- The sort logic in the controller is clunky: three when() calls that re-read the request.
- Views read request() directly.
- The shared form is an @include partial rather than a component, and the flash message appears only on the admin index.
- On the plus side, it falls back to newest for an unknown sort, uses id tie-breakers, and has nice small badge, alert and input-error components.

v.rationale: All four pass their suites and share the same Filament 5 scaffold: Schemas/Tables classes, enums with HasLabel/HasColor, a TicketPolicy where only admins may delete, and a replies relation manager that stamps the author. Probes confirmed that in every implementation a non-admin cannot force a bulk delete, that 'Assign to me' overwrites an existing assignee, and that the ticket list stays at 5 queries (relationship columns are eager-loaded). They also confirmed three shared gaps. First, any user can delete a Customer, and the cascade removes that customer's tickets. Second, resolving a ticket through the form leaves resolved_at null. Third, impl-2, impl-3 and impl-4 count reopened tickets with a stale resolved_at in the average (51h against a correct 2h); impl-1 alone filters on status as well. What separates them is smaller. impl-1 has the most user-facing bug: a duplicate customer email throws a UniqueConstraintViolationException (a 500) because the form has no unique rule, and it also has fewer validation tests. impl-2 puts its enums in the root App namespace, uses the deprecated mutateFormDataUsing, and shows 0.0 hours when nothing was resolved. impl-3 has the most thorough tests: validation datasets for every required field, exact stat values, and delete checks in both directions. It loses a little for testing the widget through invade(), a redundant widget registration and a misleading '0.0 hrs'. impl-4 is equally clean, shows N/A for the empty case and tests the widget through Livewire, but its form has no resolved_at field at all and its tests are slightly thinner. Ranking: impl-3 > impl-4 > impl-2 > impl-1. The probe test file vanished from every implementation before I could delete it myself, so no probe files are left in the repos.

v.rationale:
All four pass their own suites (impl-4 34 tests, impl-3 43, impl-2 32, impl-1 30). They follow nearly the same Filament 5 layout: enums with HasLabel and HasColor, Schemas and Tables classes, a policy that limits delete to admins, and the widget average computed in PHP. I ran the same throwaway probes against each one.

Shared defects:
- A non-admin can delete a customer, and the cascade then deletes that customer's tickets.
- Changing status in the edit form does not keep resolved_at in sync.

Relation columns do not cause N+1 queries in any of them: Filament eager-loads them automatically (checked in vendor at InteractsWithTableQuery.php:53).

What decided the ranking:
- **impl-1 (4th):** the only one with a confirmed crash. A duplicate customer email hits the database unique index and throws SQLSTATE 23000 instead of showing a form error, and there is no maxLength anywhere (a 300-character subject was accepted). It also adds view pages and infolists nobody asked for, and has the thinnest tests.
- **impl-2 (3rd):** enums sit in the App\ root namespace, it uses the legacy mutateFormDataUsing, customers.email has no database unique index, the widget shows a misleading 0.0 when empty, the widget assertions are weak, and there is no bulk-delete coverage.
- **impl-3 (2nd):** the broadest tests, with good datasets. It is the only one that keeps is_admin out of fillable. Against that, the widget test uses invade() instead of Filament's Livewire testing, the empty widget shows '0.0 hrs', the widget registration is redundant, and it has trivial enum unit tests.
- **impl-4 (1st):** the cleanest and most idiomatic Filament 5 code. It shows N/A in an empty widget, selects only the columns it needs, adds tickets_count on customers, and has typed relations. Its tests cover sorting in both directions, delete on both the table and edit page for both roles, the widget window and N/A state, and reply internal and author. Its only extra weak spot is that the form has no resolved_at field.

All four suites pass. My probes found a bug shared by all four: a 200 response that is empty or malformed overwrites the last-known rates (impl-1 writes [], impl-2/3/4 write null), so the stale fallback is lost. That bug does not change the ranking. The differences below decide it.

impl-2 ranks first. It has the cleanest modern Laravel code: a FormRequest, thin controllers, an Action, #[Scope] scopes and HasManyThrough. It re-checks the cache inside the lock and has the most thorough tests, using travel() across the flexible windows and the 1-hour expiry. Its only weakness is relying on the 5s flexible window instead of invalidating on model events.

impl-1 ranks second. It best meets the requirement that changes show within seconds, because it is the only one that invalidates on model events. Its lock tests are also good. But it has fat controllers, inline Validator::make, and API routes declared in web.php. Its invalidation misses one team's cache when a task moves between teams. And the empty-rates failure is worse here: it serves [] as fresh data.

impl-3 ranks third. It has the best stampede protection (block(5) with a re-check of the cache and handling of LockTimeoutException). Against that it has a fat controller with inline validation, an odd `json('rates') ?? json()` fallback, thinner tests and a test that really waits 5 seconds.

impl-4 ranks last despite architecture as good as impl-2's (config URL, report()). It has a real requirement bug: last-good rates expire after one day, so an outage longer than a day returns 503. It throws HttpException from a domain action, and it has a test that asserts changes appear only after 6 minutes, which contradicts the task's freshness requirement.

v.rationale: No implementation is fully correct. Two requirements separate them: invalidating the dashboard when a team's projects or tasks change ("reflected within seconds"), and preventing a stampede where concurrent cold misses still get data. impl-1 is the only one that invalidates through model events. Probes showed impls 2, 3 and 4 still serve stale counts on the first request after the 5s flexible window, and a low-traffic team can see stale data for up to 5 minutes. impl-1 still has the non-blocking-lock 503-on-cold-miss bug, and its controllers are fat with inline validation, but it meets the task's central caching requirement, so it ranks first. impl-3 is the only one using lock->block with a double-checked read, so it gets the stampede right, but it has no invalidation, weaker idioms (inline Validator, logic in the controller, hardcoded URL) and serial retries during outages. It ranks second because it has fewer real bugs than 4 and 2. impl-4 and impl-2 have the best structure (Actions, FormRequests, #[Scope], thin controllers) but both miss invalidation and both return 503 to concurrent cold misses, with tests that assert that behaviour. impl-4 edges impl-2 with a stricter regex (impl-2's 'alpha' accepted 'ÉUR' in a probe), a config-driven URL and report() on failures. impl-2 has somewhat broader rate tests, which isn't enough to outweigh that. Every implementation mishandles a malformed 200 upstream body: impl-1 caches empty rates, and the others overwrite last-known with null. All test suites pass (4: 17, 3: 16, 2: 22, 1: 21).

v.rationale:
All four suites pass: 21, 22, 18 and 19 tests. I probed each implementation with throwaway tests and deleted them afterwards. The biggest differentiator was a probe that kept the rate limiter saturated while a real database-queue worker ran the job. impl-4 uses retryUntil, so the job stayed pending and eventually processed. impl-1, impl-2 and impl-3 cap attempts with tries, and every RateLimited or WithoutOverlapping release uses one up, so healthy events get marked failed under load. impl-2 was confirmed failing with 'attempted too many times'; impl-1 and impl-3 reached their attempt caps.

impl-4 is ranked first. It is the cleanest: FormRequest validation, a policy, UniqueConstraintViolationException dedupe, a processed-state guard, and fast failure for permanent errors. Its remaining issues are small: the receipt is not queued and there is no transaction, so a retry can duplicate side effects, and unknown event types get a 422.

impl-3 is second. It has the best notification handling (queued, on-demand) and refund idempotency, and it separates 5xx from 4xx correctly. However, it has no processed guard, and my probe showed a re-run sends the receipt again. It also detects duplicates by string-matching the exception message and uses a zero-delay WithoutOverlapping release.

impl-1 is third. Its receipt dedupe and refund idempotency are good, but it retries HTTP calls inside the job with Http::retry. One rate-limit slot can then send 4 requests and block the worker for 1.2s, which breaks the explicit 10 req/s requirement. It also leaves payment_id and refund_id unvalidated, so they crash in the job, and firstOrCreate is not race-safe for duplicate deliveries.

impl-2 is last. It serves the webhook on the wrong path (/api/webhooks/payments, so the specified path returns 404). It also verifies the signature and validates inline in the controller, treats any QueryException as a duplicate, marks unknown types processed silently, uses string constants instead of enums, and returns the admin list without pagination.

v.rationale:
All four pass their own suites (13, 13, 14 and 13 tests). A shared probe (empty params, array params, invalid date combinations, same-day ranges, datetime from, case of country) decided the ranking.

impl-2 ranks first: best Laravel architecture (readonly filters DTO, #[Scope] attributes, an injected action, the filter defined once and reused as a whereIn subquery, $request->enum() for the default). Its only 500 needs an unusual array input (country[]=DK hitting strtoupper in prepareForValidation). The size:2 country rule goes beyond the spec.

impl-1 ranks second: it survived every probe without a 500 and has clean validation and good collection pipelines. It is marked down for a fat controller that eager-loads the whole order graph and aggregates in PHP, which is a real scalability flaw for a sales report, and for a whereDate string comparison against a datetime from.

impl-3 ranks third: the thin controller, action and #[Scope] are good, but a hand-rolled after() hook replacing after_or_equal returns 500 for a common input (an invalid from with a valid to). It also rejects empty optional params and adds a redundant whereHas on top of joins.

impl-4 ranks last: SQL aggregation is solid and its tests are the most thorough, but ?status= (empty) returns 500 because of 'nullable' combined with OrderStatus::from(''). The controller is fat, and the filter logic is duplicated across two builders.

v.rationale: All four suites pass: impl-1 20/20, impl-2 19/19, impl-3 22/22, impl-4 31/31. One shared probe ran against every implementation: array query params, bogus status, per_page -1 and 100000, duplicate, empty and nested tags, symbol-only titles, slug collisions and retitles, a publish-draft-republish cycle, 404, and non-owner requests with an invalid payload. The probe file was deleted afterwards. impl-2 is the only one with real runtime defects. Its index filters are unvalidated, so ?tag[]=x and ?status[]=x return 500, per_page is unbounded (and -1 returns every row on SQLite), and a bogus status is silently ignored. It also re-adds the AuthorizesRequests trait, its resource reads tags without whenLoaded, and its pivot timestamps are always null, so it ranks last. impl-1 is fully correct but puts the slug, draft-default and published_at logic in a fatter controller, with that logic repeated across store and update, so it ranks third. impl-3 and impl-4 share the same modern shape: an ObservedBy observer, #[Scope] scopes, an IndexPostRequest with per_page bounds, and the policy ->is() check. impl-4 has the richer test suite and dedupes tags. However, it passes validated() including 'tags' straight to create() and update(), which only works because non-fillable keys are silently discarded; it breaks under strict mode. It also leaves slug and published_at fillable. impl-3 uses safe()->except('tags'), restricts fillable to user-editable fields and has the thinnest controller, so it takes first place narrowly despite its slightly thinner update-tag test coverage.

v.rationale:
All four implementations pass their own suites. I added one throwaway probe test to each (duplicate or empty tags, symbol-only titles, malformed index filters, slug collision on update, a null title, a non-author sending invalid data, republishing, creating a post directly on the model, and index query count) and deleted it afterwards.

impl-4 and impl-3 are nearly the same design: a FormRequest per action, an observer, #[Scope] methods, Gate::authorize and a resource. Neither has a bug of its own. impl-4 comes first on a very small margin. Its scopes handle nullable filters themselves, it dedupes tag names, sets the status default on the model, and has the broadest tests (tag replace vs omitted tags, invalid filter). impl-3 does separate out the tags input more cleanly (safe()->except) and regenerates slugs when the title changes, but it has fewer tests (22 vs 31) and none for updating tags. impl-4's main blemish is passing 'tags' into create() and relying on Fillable to drop it.

impl-1 is correct under every probe: filters are validated, and pagination has no per_page parameter to abuse. But it is a fat controller with slug and publish logic in private methods, inline validation in index, no return types and boilerplate docblocks. The publish rule is also gated on isDirty('status').

impl-2 is last because of real defects. It does no validation on index, so ?tag[]=x, ?status[]=draft and ?per_page=-1 each return HTTP 500, per_page has no upper bound, and an invalid status silently returns an empty list. On store, status is required instead of defaulting to draft. Slug logic sits in the controller, and the factory queries the database.

One issue affects all four: an empty slug for symbol-only titles.
